title: Gold Coils Below $4,150 as Markets Await the Fed's Minutes
excerpt: Bullion slipped as the dollar and Treasury yields climbed, with traders pricing an 85% chance of a December rate hike ahead of the September FOMC minutes.
body:
• Spot gold eased 0.3% to $4,150.23 an ounce and US futures slipped 0.2% to $4,177.60 on Wednesday as investors positioned for the minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting, due later in the day.
  • The dollar index rose 0.3% and 10-year Treasury yields climbed toward a 24-year high — both classic headwinds for non-yielding bullion.
  • Traders still price an 85% chance of a rate hike by December, according to CME FedWatch, even as soft data has damped October expectations; the minutes' tone on further tightening could reshape those odds.
  • For investors: gold is boxed between a two-month low of $4,104 and resistance near $4,180. A hawkish read of the minutes would lift yields and the dollar and could drag gold back toward $4,000 — the level analysts say would likely attract staggered, conviction-based buying.

Gold spent Wednesday holding its breath. Prices slipped as investors turned their attention to the minutes of the US Federal Reserve's September meeting, due later in the day, hunting for any hint that policymakers remain inclined to raise interest rates further.

Spot gold eased 0.3% to $4,150.23 an ounce by 0145 GMT, while US gold futures edged 0.2% lower to $4,177.60, according to Reuters. In European trading, selling intensified — gold fell more than 1% to $4,122.75 from an opening level of $4,164.68, after recording a high of $4,170.03, resuming losses after a brief pause on Tuesday that had delivered the metal's first advance in three sessions.

The dollar and yields squeeze bullion

The pressure on gold came from two familiar sources. The US Dollar Index rose 0.3%, making greenback-priced metals more expensive for buyers holding other currencies, and the 10-year Treasury yield resumed its climb toward a 24-year high. In a high-rate environment, investors tend to favour yield-generating assets over a metal that pays nothing.

"The yellow metal is likely to remain relatively stable with a mild downside bias," said Frank Walbaum, a market analyst at Naga.com. "Minutes will clarify the Fed's monetary policy and the degree of support among policymakers for further rate increases and could reshape upcoming hike odds."

"Minutes will clarify the Fed's monetary policy and the degree of support among policymakers for further rate increases and could reshape upcoming hike odds."

— Frank Walbaum, market analyst at Naga.com

The Wall Street Journal's market live blog noted that Tuesday's advance to $4,180 was met with fresh selling as oil prices rebounded and long-end bond yields stayed near multiyear highs, with the dollar index up at 102.19. Phillip Nova analyst Priyanka Sachdeva argued the metal's structural drivers — geopolitical uncertainty, fragile Middle Eastern oil flows — have not disappeared, and that $4,000 remains the key level where staggered buying could return.

What the minutes could change

The September meeting minutes matter because the Fed's intentions are genuinely ambiguous. San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly has said whether further rate hikes are needed depends largely on whether the factors pushing up inflation fade or persist, while Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid has argued rates still need to rise further to bring inflation down.

Recent soft economic data has dampened expectations of an October rate increase — traders price an 85% chance the Fed stands pat then — but still see an 85% chance of a hike by December, according to CME's FedWatch tool. If the minutes show broad support for further tightening, that December probability hardens and real yields climb, squeezing gold. If they reveal hesitation or disagreement, yields and the dollar could ease, giving the metal breathing room even with a December hike still on the table.

Elsewhere in metals, spot silver fell roughly 1% to $61.12, platinum rose 0.2% to $1,704.25, and palladium lost 0.3% to $1,168.20.

A crowded year for gold

The current slide follows a rough September in which gold fell 6%, and Wednesday's levels sit just above the two-month low of $4,104.15 touched on Tuesday. That correction has barely dented the optimism of the industry's long-term bulls: delegates at the London Bullion Market Association's annual conference in Sorrento, Italy, forecast that gold could reach $5,013 an ounce over the next 12 months, according to Reuters.

The macro overlay is complicated by geopolitics. Brent crude climbed above $100 a barrel as elevated energy prices fanned inflation worries and clouded the fiscal outlook, reinforcing expectations of a prolonged higher-rate environment — a backdrop that cuts both ways for gold, lifting safe-haven interest while strengthening the dollar that weighs on it.

What investors should watch

The minutes land this afternoon US time, and the market's reaction will likely show up first in the bond and currency markets rather than in gold itself. A hawkish tone that pushes the 10-year yield to new multiyear highs and the dollar higher would keep gold on the defensive. A dovish surprise — real disagreement about further hikes, concern about growth — could let the metal recover toward $4,180 and beyond.

For Indian investors watching alongside, the global pullback contrasts with domestic strength: 24-karat gold in India was trading around Rs 1.49 lakh per 10 grams earlier this week as festive-season buying began. How much of that Indian demand offsets the global macro headwinds will shape where the metal goes next.
